objection: Was Jesus made God at the Council of Nicaea?
answer:
I understand why that story is appealing — it lets you sidestep an uncomfortable claim by treating it as a late invention. But I'd gently push back: what you've heard has the history backwards, and it's worth wanting the truth here, not the comfort.

The Council of Nicaea in 325 didn't vote Jesus into divinity; it defended a confession already ancient. The bishops there weren't inventing anything — they were answering Arius, who taught the Son was the highest creature, made before time but still made ("there was when He was not"). Nicaea's answer, homoousios, "of one essence" with the Father, canonized what was already confessed in the Philippian hymn and by Ignatius, writers reaching back into the first Christian generation. That's the key point: the confession of Jesus as Lord and God is embedded in the oldest material the New Testament contains — predating even Paul's own letters — and it's the assumed faith of the century of Christian writers after the apostles, men like Ignatius, Justin, and Irenaeus, who saw themselves as defending the Jesus already worshipped, not introducing a new one.

Even the risen Lord's own command to baptize in the one name of Father, Son, and Holy Ghost (Matthew 28:19), and Paul's threefold benediction (2 Corinthians 13:14), show this pattern stamped on the church from its very threshold. Nicaea is a guardrail fencing in a faith already prayed, not a coup installing a new one. So when Thomas cries "My Lord and my God" in John 20:28, or Paul says the fulness of the Godhead dwells bodily in Christ (Colossians 2:9), you're not looking at fourth-century theology read backward — you're looking at what the earliest disciples themselves concluded, staring at the man in front of them.

transcript.content: I've heard this one before — that the Council of Nicaea basically *invented* the idea that Jesus is God, and that the early church actually saw him as just a really exceptional human or prophet elevated to divinity later. Is that true? Because if it is, it feels like the whole foundation shifts: were the first disciples even claiming he *was* God, or did that get added in by church politics centuries later? I want to believe this, but I *want* it to be true based on what the apostles actually taught, not based on what some council decided.
